primaryText: He might get sick tomorrow.
translation: He might get sick tomorrow.
comment: A modal for the present with an eventive predicate and a future frame adverbial. The paper lists must, ought to, should, may and might alike; might stands for all.

primaryText: He might get sick now.
translation: He might get sick now.
comment: A modal for the present with an eventive predicate and a present frame adverbial. Marked ?? in the paper: the event must fall within the present, which the semantics does not exclude.

primaryText: He might get sick yesterday.
translation: He might get sick yesterday.
comment: A modal for the present with an eventive predicate and a past frame adverbial.

primaryText: He might be getting sick now.
translation: He might be getting sick now.
comment: A modal for the present with a progressive, hence stative, predicate and a present frame adverbial.

primaryText: He might be getting sick yesterday.
translation: He might be getting sick yesterday.
comment: A modal for the present with a progressive predicate and a past frame adverbial.

primaryText: He might be sick now.
translation: He might be sick now.
comment: A modal for the present with a stative predicate and a present frame adverbial. Against Enç's shifting modals: the same modal is non-shifting here and shifting with tomorrow.

primaryText: He might be sick tomorrow.
translation: He might be sick tomorrow.
comment: A modal for the present with a stative predicate and a future frame adverbial.

primaryText: He might be sick yesterday.
translation: He might be sick yesterday.
comment: A modal for the present with a stative predicate and a past frame adverbial.

primaryText: He must have gotten sick yesterday.
translation: He must have gotten sick yesterday.
comment: A modal for the past, the modal over the perfect, with an eventive predicate and a past frame adverbial. The paper lists must, ought to, should, may and might alike; must stands for all, since only the subjunctive-form modals also scope under the perfect, [34].

primaryText: He must have gotten sick tomorrow.
translation: He must have gotten sick tomorrow.
comment: A modal for the past with an eventive predicate and a future frame adverbial. The paper sets aside the future perfect reading, as in 'he may have arrived by next week'. With might the perfect-over-modal scoping of [34] would rescue the sentence.

primaryText: He must have been sick yesterday.
translation: He must have been sick yesterday.
comment: A modal for the past with a stative predicate and a past frame adverbial.

primaryText: He must have been sick tomorrow.
translation: He must have been sick tomorrow.
comment: A modal for the past with a stative predicate and a future frame adverbial.

primaryText: He may have won yesterday.
translation: He may have won yesterday.
comment: PRES(MAY(PERF(YESTERDAY(he win)))): the winning lies within an interval preceding the forward interval of the present and within yesterday. Derived in the paper's [30]-[31].

primaryText: He may win yesterday.
translation: He may win yesterday.
comment: PRES(MAY(YESTERDAY(he win))): the winning must lie within the intersection of the forward interval of the present with yesterday, the null interval. Derived in the paper's [32]: never true, hence deviant.

primaryText: He might have been available yesterday.
translation: He might have been available yesterday.
comment: A modal that can scope under the perfect, on the counterfactual scoping, with a past frame adverbial.

primaryText: He might have been available next month.
translation: He might have been available next month.
comment: The perfect over the modal: the reference interval starts at a past time and extends to the end of time, admitting a future frame adverbial.

primaryText: It might have been raining yesterday.
translation: It might have been raining yesterday.
comment: The perfect over the modal with a past frame adverbial.

primaryText: It might have been raining now.
translation: It might have been raining now.
comment: The perfect over the modal with a present frame adverbial.

primaryText: He must have been available yesterday.
translation: He must have been available yesterday.
comment: Must only scopes over the perfect; a past frame adverbial.

primaryText: He must have been available next month.
translation: He must have been available next month.
comment: Must only scopes over the perfect, whose reference interval precedes the present; a future frame adverbial. Only modals in the subjunctive form, might, would, should, ought to, scope under the perfect.

primaryText: It must have been raining yesterday.
translation: It must have been raining yesterday.
comment: Must over the perfect with a past frame adverbial.

primaryText: It must have been raining now.
translation: It must have been raining now.
comment: Must over the perfect with a present frame adverbial.

primaryText: He may win the game.
translation: He may win the game.
comment: A modal for the present: the possibility is from the perspective of the present about the future, and the modality can be epistemic or metaphysical.

primaryText: He may have (already) won the game (# but he didn't).
translation: He may have (already) won the game (# but he didn't).
comment: The epistemic reading of a modal for the past: the modal over the perfect, perspective the present, orientation past; the issue is settled and the speaker does not know which way. The continuation 'but he didn't' is infelicitous on this reading.

primaryText: At that point he might (still) have won the game but he didn't in the end.
translation: At that point he might (still) have won the game but he didn't in the end.
comment: The counterfactual reading of a modal for the past: the perfect over the modal, perspective a past time, orientation that time's future; the modality is metaphysical. Mondadori's future in the past.

primaryText: He may/might have the flu (now).
translation: He may/might have the flu (now).
comment: A modal for the present with a stative predicate on the reading where reference is to the present: only epistemic, since whether he has the flu now is settled by the course of events.

primaryText: He may/might get the flu.
translation: He may/might get the flu.
comment: A modal for the present with an eventive predicate: reference to the future, and a metaphysical as well as an epistemic reading.

primaryText: It hasn't been decided yet who he will meet with. He may see the dean. He may see the provost.
translation: It hasn't been decided yet who he will meet with. He may see the dean. He may see the provost.
context: He will meet with one senior administrator.
comment: The issue is asserted not to be settled, and the modals get a metaphysical interpretation.

primaryText: It has been decided who he will meet with but I don't know who it is. He may see the dean. He may see the provost.
translation: It has been decided who he will meet with but I don't know who it is. He may see the dean. He may see the provost.
context: He will meet with one senior administrator.
comment: The issue is asserted to have been settled, so after the first sentence settledness is presupposed and the modals have an epistemic reading. Future instantiation is settled only when the context contains information to that effect.

primaryText: He already returned.
translation: He already returned.
comment: Already directly on an eventive predicate. Marked ?* in the paper, between questionable and starred.

primaryText: He did not write us yet.
translation: He did not write us yet.
comment: Yet directly on an eventive predicate. Marked ?* in the paper, between questionable and starred.

primaryText: He has already returned.
translation: He has already returned.
comment: Already on the perfect of an eventive predicate, a property of times.

primaryText: He has not written us yet.
translation: He has not written us yet.
comment: Yet on the perfect of an eventive predicate.

primaryText: He might have already returned.
translation: He might have already returned.
comment: A modal for the past with already: MODAL(ALREADY(PERF(he return))), the adverb scoping between the modal and the perfect. The paper lists must, should, might and may alike. The evidence that the auxiliary have is a perfect, not a past tense.

primaryText: He might not have written us yet.
translation: He might not have written us yet.
comment: A modal for the past with yet between the modal and the perfect.

primaryText: He might already return.
translation: He might already return.
comment: A modal for the present with already on an eventive predicate: no perfect to satisfy the sortal restriction.

primaryText: He might not write us yet.
translation: He might not write us yet.
comment: A modal for the present with yet on an eventive predicate. On a deontic construal of the modal yet is acceptable; the paper sets root modals aside.

primaryText: He might still win.
translation: He might still win.
comment: PRES(STILL(MIGHT(he win))): still scopes over the possibility modal, presupposing that the possibility of his winning was a live option before. The temporal, not the concessive, reading of still.

primaryText: At that point he might still have won.
translation: At that point he might still have won.
comment: PRES(PERF(STILL(MIGHT(he win)))): still scopes over the modal and under the perfect on the counterfactual reading.

primaryText: He may still win.
translation: He may still win.
comment: STILL over MAY: presupposes the possibility was live and asserts it persists, consistent with possibilities decreasing over time.

primaryText: He may already win.
translation: He may already win.
comment: ALREADY over MAY: presupposes the possibility was not live and asserts it has become so, inconsistent with possibilities decreasing over time; already cannot scope under the modal, since its complement is eventive.

primaryText: Er könnte (schon) gewonnen haben.
translation: He might have (already) won.
comment: German mirrors semantic scope in the linear order of the modal and the perfect auxiliary: the modal over the perfect, the epistemic reading only. Schon requires MODAL > ALREADY > PERF, which this order allows.

primaryText: Er hätte schon gewinnen können.
translation: He might have already won.
comment: The perfect over the modal with schon.

primaryText: Er hätte (noch) gewinnen können.
translation: He might (still) have won.
comment: The perfect over the modal, the counterfactual reading only. Noch requires PERF > STILL > MODAL, which this order allows.

primaryText: Er könnte noch gewonnen haben.
translation: He might still have won.
comment: The modal over the perfect with noch.
